title: Colona Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Colona wells have a 244 ft median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $18,200-$30,300.
h1: Colona, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Colona sits in a mixed sedimentary and alluvial groundwater setting, with most permitted wells identified as unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. Records within 5 miles show a wide spread in depth and production. That matters when you are pricing a homesite: nearby wells provide useful local guidance, but they do not guarantee the result on a particular lot.

There are 308 Colorado DWR permits in this area, including 182 recorded as constructed. Only 53 report a pump yield and 15 report a static water level, so the most useful numbers are patterns rather than promises. Review the permit file, neighboring wells, and the proposed septic and building layout before committing to land.

sections.heading: How deep are Colona wells?
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Colona is 244 feet. The middle half runs from 92 to 361 feet, which is a substantial spread for estimating a drilling bid. The 90th percentile reaches 596 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 840 feet.

Depth is distributed across the area: 27% of wells are under 100 feet, 32% fall from 100 to 300 feet, 31% from 300 to 600 feet, and 10% exceed 600 feet. For a buyer, the median is a starting point, not a ceiling. Mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground can change the drilling approach and final depth from one parcel to the next.

sections.heading: What Colona wells produce
sections.html:
Among the 53 wells that report pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 4.0 to 12.0 gallons per minute. The records show 6% under 1 gallon per minute, 21% from 1 to 5, 55% from 5 to 15, and 19% above 15.

That distribution is generally workable for a household, but a reported yield is not the same as storage, pressure, or dependable long-term supply. Ask for the actual well construction and pump information. A low-producing well may still serve a home with suitable tank storage, while irrigation or stock use can require a different water-rights review.

sections.heading: Water levels around Colona
sections.html:
The 15 reported static water levels have a median depth to water of 144 feet. The middle half ranges from 67 to 179 feet below ground. Those figures help a contractor think about pump setting, trenching, and electrical work, but they are not a complete groundwater trend.

There are too few reported static levels to conclude from these records alone that the water table is dropping or stable. Water levels can vary with season, nearby pumping, and the aquifer intercepted by the well. Have the driller check current conditions and compare the closest completed wells rather than relying only on the area median.

sections.heading: Colona permit history and drillers
sections.html:
Permits were issued throughout the area’s recorded history, with 8 in the 1950s, 4 in the 1960s, 36 in the 1970s, 34 in the 1980s, 46 in the 1990s, 52 in the 2000s, 21 in the 2010s, and 24 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. Domestic or household use accounts for 69% of permits, while stock use accounts for 25%.

Valley Drilling Co. (Stoy, Kenneth) appears most often, with 60 records. Western Drilling Services, Llc (Kuchler, Richard A.) has 15, and Groundwater Dev. Inc. (Kuchler, Michael S.) has 14. These records show local experience, not a guarantee of availability or price.

sections.heading: What a new Colona well can cost
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a drilling rate of $50 to $75 per foot for mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 244-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $12,200 to $18,300.

A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $18,200 to $30,300. A deeper-than-median hole, difficult access, casing or grout requirements, or changes to the site plan can move the bid higher. Get the drilling scope in writing and ask what happens if the hole is dry or produces less than expected.

Before construction, confirm the permit requirements with Colorado DWR. An exempt household-use well still has defined limits, including the 35 gpm exempt-well pumping limit, and an over-appropriated basin may require an augmentation plan.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building near Colona
sections.html:
Low yield and dry-hole risk deserve attention because depth and production vary widely. The aquifer names on permits are mostly unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, with 287 wells in that category. Fractured rock can be unpredictable: a nearby successful well does not prove the same result on your lot.

Environmental screening also matters. Within about 10 miles, the records show 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site and 6 historic mine features, with 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not establish contamination at a parcel. Test the water after construction and check local site history.

Keep the well, septic system, replacement area, access, and house location coordinated. Confirm setbacks, drainage, casing and grout details, and year-round access for a drill rig and service truck before buying or grading.

sections.heading: Buying land around Colona
sections.html:
Start with the closest completed wells, not just the regional median. The area includes Loghill Village, Montrose, Ridgway, Portland, Ouray, and Olathe, but conditions can change quickly across those broader surroundings. Within the Colona search area, compare depth, reported yield, static water level, use, and aquifer description for parcels that resemble the one you are considering.

For a new homesite, make the well permit, septic feasibility, driveway access, and house location part of the same review. Budget around the local cost model while allowing for a deeper hole or difficult site. A Colorado driller can also explain casing, grout, pump sizing, and what testing is appropriate after completion.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Colona, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth near Colona is 244 feet. The middle half of wells runs from 92 to 361 feet, while the 90th percentile is 596 feet and the deepest recorded well is 840 feet. The spread is wide enough that nearby well records should guide a site-specific drilling estimate.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Colona?
faq.a: The local drilling model is $50 to $75 per foot. At the 244-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $12,200 to $18,300. A finished system, including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, is modeled at about $18,200 to $30,300. Access, depth, and construction requirements can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Colona wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 53 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 4.0 to 12.0 gallons per minute. Records show 6% under 1 gallon per minute. Yield is not the same as storage or pressure, so review the well test and pump setup.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Colona, Colorado?
faq.a: The area has 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site and 6 historic mine features within about 10 miles, with 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those area records do not determine water quality at a specific parcel. Test a private well after completion and review the property’s nearby land and mine history.

faq.q: Should I check a well before buying land near Colona?
faq.a: Yes. The records include 308 permits, but only 182 are recorded as constructed, 53 report pump yield, and 15 report static water level. Compare the closest completed wells and confirm the permit, septic layout, access, and building location. A local driller can identify whether fractured-bedrock conditions increase uncertainty.
